## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="t13-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>What to build</dt><dd>Seven numbers: MW of five plants and the battery's MW and MWh; each costs money every year.</dd>
<dt>Hourly operation</dt><dd>Given what is built, the solver runs the plants and the battery at least cost each hour.</dd>
<dt>Seven weeks</dt><dd>Four typical weeks and three extreme ones stand for the 52 weeks of 2025.</dd>
<dt>Storage link</dt><dd>The battery's charge carries from each calendar week to the next.</dd>
<dt>CO₂ cap</dt><dd>An extra rule; its shadow price is the cost of the last tonne cut.</dd>
<dt>Frontier</dt><dd>The cheapest plan at each CO₂ level; no plan is both cheaper and cleaner.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<style>/* lesson-local: keep Go deeper text inside the card on phones; wide equations and tables scroll on their own */.page-lesson .lx-deeper-body{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr)}.page-lesson .lx-deeper-body .math.display{display:block;overflow-x:auto;overflow-y:hidden}.page-lesson .lx-deeper-body table{display:block;overflow-x:auto}.lx13-fallback td,.lx13-fallback th{font-size:13.5px}</style>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The capstone as a linear program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The decisions are the capacities $K_i$ (MW, and MWh for the battery's energy) and, for every modelled hour $t$, the gas outputs $g_t, q_t$, the battery's charge $c_t$ and discharge $d_t$, its level $s_t$ and the unserved demand $u_t$. With $a^{w}_t, a^{s}_t$ the wind and solar output per MW built, $D_t$ the demand and $w_t$ the hours of the year each modelled hour stands for:

$$\min \; \sum_i f_i K_i + \sum_t w_t \big(r_\mathrm{cc}\, g_t + r_\mathrm{pk}\, q_t + V u_t\big)$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{w}_t K_\mathrm{wind} + a^{s}_t K_\mathrm{solar} + 0.911\,K_\mathrm{nuc} + g_t + q_t + d_t - c_t + u_t &\ge D_t && \text{(demand)}\\
g_t \le K_\mathrm{cc}, \quad q_t \le K_\mathrm{pk}, \quad c_t + d_t &\le K_\mathrm{bp} && \text{(sizes)}\\
s_t = s_{t-1} + 0.85\,c_t - d_t, \qquad 0 \le s_t &\le K_\mathrm{be} && \text{(battery)}\\
\textstyle\sum_t w_t\,(0.329\, g_t + 0.484\, q_t) &\le \text{cap} && \text{(CO}_2\text{)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The yearly cost of a plant is its capital cost times the [capital recovery factor]{.lx-term term="capital-recovery-factor"}, plus fixed O&M; at a 4% real cost of capital over 30 years the factor is 0.0578. Running cost is heat rate times fuel price plus variable O&M:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{wind, per kW-year:}\;\; & 1{,}712 \times 0.0578 + 34.57 = \$133.6\\
\text{combined-cycle, per MWh:}\;\; & 6.226 \times \$3.85 + \$3.49 = \$27.46\\
\text{its CO}_2\text{, t per MWh:}\;\; & 6.226 \times 0.05291 = 0.329
\end{aligned}
$$

Every term is linear, so this is a [linear program]{.lx-term term="linear-program"}. Your plan fixes the $K_i$ and leaves only the hourly decisions; the optimizer chooses both, with $u_t = 0$. Upcoming: M3 (capacity expansion) writes the same model in code.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Seven weeks for a year: how, and how well</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Each season's [representative week]{.lx-term term="representative-period"} is its medoid: the real week closest, hour by hour, to all the season's other weeks, scaled so the season keeps its demand, wind and solar energy. It stands for 12 (winter), 14 (spring), 10 (summer) or 13 (fall) weeks. Three weeks are kept as they were: the year's peak demand, the peak of demand minus wind and sun, and the least wind.

The battery's level is linked across the calendar (after Kotzur and co-authors, 2018): week $i$ starts at $S_i$, and its representative week $k$ adds its net change $\Delta_k$, so $S_{i+1} = S_i + \Delta_k$; its lowest and highest swing, $\ell_k$ and $h_k$, must keep $0 \le S_i + \ell_k$ and $S_i + h_k \le K_\mathrm{be}$. The year ends where it began.

The check: the optimizer's plans, rounded up to the sliders' steps, re-run hour by hour on all 8,760 hours.

| Plan | Cost, 7 weeks | Cost, full year | CO₂, 7 weeks | CO₂, full year | Unserved, full year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Optimizer at 400 kt | $118.8M | $118.9M | 390 kt | 391 kt | 0 MWh |
| Optimizer at 200 kt | $128.6M | $130.1M | 189 kt | 208 kt | 67 MWh |
| Optimizer at 100 kt | $142.4M | $145.2M | 95 kt | 128 kt | 101 MWh |

Solving the optimizer itself on all 8,760 hours gives the same plan with no cap, but the cheapest 200 kt plan then costs $133.2M, 5% more, and its last tonne $139 instead of $73. Shallow cuts survive the check; deep cuts do not quite: seven weeks miss some still, hot evenings, so the plan emits more and goes short. Planners respond with more or longer periods, extreme weeks and adequacy tests over many weather years (A5, upcoming).

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="t13-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wind-alone" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If wind is the cheapest way to cut CO₂, the cheapest clean plan is all wind.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. On still evenings the town still needs firm plants or storage; at 100 kt the optimizer keeps 250 MW of gas and adds solar and a battery.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="spill" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The cheapest plan never spills any wind or sun.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At a 100 kt cap the optimizer spills 9% on purpose: extra wind is cheaper than storing every last MWh.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="weeks" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Seven well-chosen weeks give exactly the same answer as the whole year.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Re-run on all 8,760 hours, the optimizer's 200 kt plan emits 208 kt and leaves 67 MWh unserved.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="t13">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="gap" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Your plan costs $140.0M a year and emits 150 kt. The cheapest plan at 150 kt costs $131.4M. How far above the frontier are you?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">8.6%</li><li data-value="b">6.5%</li><li data-value="c">$8.6M</li><li data-value="d">150 kt</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>6.5%: 140.0 ÷ 131.4 − 1 = 0.065. You could cut cost by $8.6M a year with the same CO₂.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

<p>Real planning studies solve this same problem with many regions, transmission between them and decades of investment. NLR's open <a href="https://www.nlr.gov/analysis/reeds/">ReEDS model</a> plans the contiguous U.S. power system this way; <a href="https://docs.pypsa.org/">PyPSA</a> is an open Python framework for the same kind of study.</p>
</div>
